name: Hyraceum

lead: Hyraceum is the hardened, petrified urine and droppings of the rock hyrax, a small southern African and Middle Eastern mammal that uses the same rock latrines for generations. Perfumers prize it, often sold as 'Africa Stone', for an animalic, fermented, musky scent often compared to castoreum and civet.

Its appearance angle is fragrance: a scent that smells warm and skin-like can add to how a person comes across. It has also been used in traditional Cape medicine, and a few laboratory and pilot studies have looked at its chemistry and at related scents. None tests it as a cosmetic.

paras: In perfumery it is typically processed into a tincture or absolute that is blended into fragrance as a fixative and animalic accent. Fragrance hobbyists and niche perfumers use it as a substitute for animal-derived musk. Wearers apply the finished fragrance in the usual way.

It is a natural material of variable composition, and fragrance ingredients can cause skin sensitivity in some people. Conservation-minded scientists object to commercial collection because middens accumulate very slowly and hold paleoenvironmental records. Traditional medicinal uses are not established clinical treatments.

angle.text: Perfumers use hyraceum as a base note that gives fragrances a warm, musky depth, so a wearer smells distinctive. The link to looks is through grooming and personal presentation rather than a direct change to the body.

lead: Hyraceum is the fossilized urine and faeces of the rock hyrax (Procavia capensis) and related species, which deposit waste in the same sheltered sites over generations until the material hardens into rock-like middens [1]. In perfumery it is known as 'Africa Stone' and is valued for an animalic, fermented, musky scent that blends notes compared to musk, castoreum, civet, tobacco and agarwood [1].

For people interested in how they smell, it is an ingredient in niche and natural fragrance, where perfumers use it as a plant-free-looking, animal-harm-free alternative to deer musk and civet [1][2]. Its warm, leathery character is used to give a scent depth and skin-like presence.

Hyraceum also has a history in Cape herbal medicine, where it is recorded among the materia medica of the Khoi-San and Cape Dutch [3]. Laboratory work has examined its chemistry and receptor activity [1][4], and a pilot study has compared the effects of a musky 'African stone' scent with lavender on anxiety measures [5].

paras: Rock hyraxes live in colonies and use communal latrines in rock crevices. Over time the combined waste crystallizes and hardens, and deposits can build up for tens of thousands of years [1]. The result is a brittle, resinous, dark brown to black material that is dug from middens [1].

Perfumers treat hyraceum as a natural animalic ingredient with an aroma often compared with castoreum and civet, and it is used as an alternative to animal-derived musk [1][2]. Sources describe the harvest as not harming live animals [1][2].

A review of Khoi-San and Cape Dutch medical ethnobotany lists hyraceum among the roughly 170 items of the recorded Cape materia medica up to 1932 and notes that most plants and hyraceum are still widely used today, especially in rural areas [3]. Reported uses include treatment of epilepsy and convulsions [1][2]. In one test of 14 samples, four showed affinity for the GABA-benzodiazepine receptor, while water extracts were inactive [1].

Because middens accumulate very slowly they are effectively non-renewable, and they preserve pollen and chemical records of past climate in arid regions [1]. Scientists have criticized commercial collection for destroying that resource [1].

No studies found of hyraceum used as a cosmetic or fragrance for appearance. Related laboratory work includes a 2026 study that characterized hippuric acid derivatives from hyraceum and tested antimicrobial activity in vitro with computational modelling [4]. A 2025 pilot study of 20 healthy participants compared lavender with a musky 'African stone' scent; the African stone scent did not change self-reported anxiety but changed EEG and heart-rate-variability measures [5]. The study concerns a scent labelled African stone and does not state that it contained hyraceum.
